counties.name: Dallas County
counties.blurb: The urban core of the Metroplex, with housing stock spanning nearly a century.
counties.context: Dallas County covers the widest range of residential roofing conditions in North Texas — prewar homes in the older neighborhoods, an enormous inventory of 1950s through 1980s suburban construction in Garland, Mesquite, Irving, and the southern cities, and infill and rebuild activity closer in. Older roofs here frequently sit under mature tree canopy, which brings debris load in valleys and limb contact into almost every inspection.

counties.name: Tarrant County
counties.blurb: Fort Worth and the Mid-Cities, on the western edge of the hail corridor.
counties.context: Tarrant County sits further west, which generally means it meets incoming spring storm systems earlier than the eastern side of the Metroplex. The Mid-Cities — Hurst, Euless, Bedford, and their neighbors — hold a dense band of 1970s and 1980s housing that is well past its first roof and often past its second. Fort Worth itself ranges from historic neighborhoods to large newer developments on the north and far west sides.

counties.name: Collin County
counties.blurb: The fastest-growing corridor in North Texas, with a huge cohort of roofs aging together.
counties.context: Collin County's residential build-out came in distinct waves, which has an unusual consequence for roofing: entire subdivisions hit the twenty-year mark within a season or two of each other. Plano's 1980s and 1990s neighborhoods, Frisco and Allen's 2000s expansion, and the newer Prosper and Celina construction each represent a different roof age band, and the storm exposure across them is broadly similar.

counties.name: Denton County
counties.blurb: From the university city down through the fast-growing 380 and 121 corridors.
counties.context: Denton County combines an established college town with some of the most aggressive suburban growth in the state along the Lewisville Lake corridor. Wind exposure is a real consideration here — open terrain on the north and west sides of the county gives storms a clear run at rooflines, and lakeside neighborhoods see it worse.

counties.name: Rockwall County
counties.blurb: Lakeside communities on the eastern edge of the Metroplex.
counties.context: Texas's smallest county by area, built around Lake Ray Hubbard. Homes with open exposure to the lake take more direct wind than their inland neighbors, and the steeper, more cut-up rooflines common in the newer lakeside developments concentrate water into valleys that need to be detailed correctly.

counties.name: Ellis County
counties.blurb: South of Dallas along the I-35E corridor, with historic housing stock and new growth.
counties.context: Ellis County pairs a genuinely historic core — Waxahachie's Victorian district is one of the most intact in Texas — with rapid newer development around Midlothian and Red Oak. Older homes here often carry complex rooflines, steep pitches, and detailing that requires a different approach than a modern production build.

counties.name: Kaufman County
counties.blurb: Southeast of Dallas, growing quickly along US 80.
counties.context: Kaufman County has absorbed substantial growth pushing east out of Dallas County, particularly around Forney and Terrell. Newer subdivisions here sit on relatively open land with limited mature tree cover, which means less debris in the gutters and more direct wind on the roof.

counties.name: Parker County
counties.blurb: West of Fort Worth, where the Metroplex gives way to open country.
counties.context: Parker County is where suburban development thins into acreage. Homes on larger lots with little windbreak see stronger sustained wind loads, and outbuildings, barns, and long fence lines are a normal part of the exterior conversation here in a way they are not inside Loop 12.

counties.name: Johnson County
counties.blurb: South of Fort Worth along the I-35W corridor.
counties.context: Johnson County covers Burleson's steady suburban growth and Cleburne's older established housing. The county's position on the southwestern approach to the Metroplex puts it in the path of storm systems tracking northeast, and it regularly sees hail before the urban core does.

counties.name: Wise County
counties.blurb: Northwest of the Metroplex, rural with growing residential pockets.
counties.context: Wise County's residential work is spread across small towns and acreage properties. Open terrain means wind is the dominant exterior concern, and metal outbuildings, long fence runs, and detached structures come up as often as the house itself.

counties.name: Hunt County
counties.blurb: Northeast along I-30, anchored by Greenville.
counties.context: Hunt County sits on the northeastern storm track out of the Metroplex and has taken significant hail events. Greenville's older residential neighborhoods hold a lot of mid-century housing that has been through multiple roof cycles, and the surrounding communities are largely rural with acreage properties.

counties.name: Grayson County
counties.blurb: The northern edge of North Texas, on the Oklahoma line.
counties.context: Grayson County covers Sherman and Denison at the top of the region, roughly an hour north of the Dallas core. Recent industrial investment has driven new residential construction alongside a large stock of older housing, and the county's position near the Red River puts it under storms that have already crossed open country.

counties.name: Hood County
counties.blurb: Southwest of Fort Worth, centered on Lake Granbury.
counties.context: Hood County's residential base is heavily weighted toward lakeside and retirement communities around Granbury. Waterfront exposure means wind is a constant factor, and many properties combine a primary residence with detached structures, decks, and long fence lines.

counties.name: Cooke County
counties.blurb: North along I-35 toward the Oklahoma border.
counties.context: Cooke County is roughly an hour and a half north of Dallas, with Gainesville as its center and a largely rural surrounding area of ranch and acreage property.

counties.name: Fannin County
counties.blurb: Northeast of the Metroplex near the Red River.
counties.context: Fannin County is rural and agricultural, with Bonham as its seat, sitting well inside the northeastern storm track that regularly delivers hail to North Texas.

counties.name: Navarro County
counties.blurb: South along I-45 toward Houston.
counties.context: Navarro County centers on Corsicana, about an hour south of Dallas, with a historic downtown and a residential stock that includes substantial older housing.

counties.name: Hill County
counties.blurb: South along I-35 between DFW and Waco.
counties.context: Hill County sits at the I-35 split roughly an hour and a quarter south of Dallas, and is heavily rural outside of Hillsboro and Whitney.

counties.name: Van Zandt County
counties.blurb: East along I-20, known for Canton's trade days.
counties.context: Van Zandt County is about an hour east of Dallas, rural in character with pockets of residential development around Canton and Wills Point.

counties.name: Henderson County
counties.blurb: Southeast of Dallas around Cedar Creek Lake.
counties.context: Henderson County's residential base includes a significant number of lake properties around Cedar Creek, where wind exposure and detached structures are common considerations.

counties.name: Hopkins County
counties.blurb: Northeast along I-30.
counties.context: Hopkins County is roughly ninety minutes northeast of Dallas along I-30, centered on Sulphur Springs and surrounded by dairy and ranch country.

counties.name: Rains County
counties.blurb: Northeast near Lake Fork.
counties.context: Rains County is small and rural, with much of its residential activity connected to Lake Fork and Lake Tawakoni recreation property.

counties.name: Delta County
counties.blurb: Small rural county northeast of the Metroplex.
counties.context: Delta County is one of the least populated counties in the region, largely agricultural, with Cooper as its seat.

counties.name: Lamar County
counties.blurb: Far northeast on the Red River.
counties.context: Lamar County centers on Paris, close to two hours northeast of Dallas, with a notable stock of historic housing and surrounding rural property.

counties.name: Red River County
counties.blurb: Far northeast corner of the region.
counties.context: Red River County sits at the outer edge of a two-hour radius from Dallas and is predominantly rural.

counties.name: Somervell County
counties.blurb: Southwest near the Brazos River.
counties.context: Somervell County is the second-smallest county in Texas by area, centered on Glen Rose, with tourism and acreage property driving much of its residential base.

counties.name: Erath County
counties.blurb: Southwest, anchored by Stephenville.
counties.context: Erath County is a university and dairy county roughly ninety minutes southwest of Fort Worth, with substantial rural and acreage property.

counties.name: Palo Pinto County
counties.blurb: West around Possum Kingdom Lake.
counties.context: Palo Pinto County includes Mineral Wells and the Possum Kingdom Lake area, where lake-property wind exposure is a defining exterior condition.

counties.name: Jack County
counties.blurb: Northwest of Fort Worth, rural.
counties.context: Jack County is sparsely populated ranch country roughly ninety minutes northwest of Fort Worth.

counties.name: Montague County
counties.blurb: Northwest on the Oklahoma border.
counties.context: Montague County is rural, with Bowie and Nocona as its principal communities, near the outer edge of a comfortable service radius.

counties.name: Clay County
counties.blurb: Far northwest, near Wichita Falls.
counties.context: Clay County lies beyond most of the Metroplex service radius, close to Wichita Falls and predominantly rural.

counties.name: Archer County
counties.blurb: Far northwest ranch country.
counties.context: Archer County is remote from the Metroplex and would fall at or past the practical edge of a two-hour radius.

counties.name: Young County
counties.blurb: Northwest, centered on Graham.
counties.context: Young County sits well west of the Metroplex and would generally require a project of significant scope to be practical.

counties.name: Stephens County
counties.blurb: West Texas edge of the service radius.
counties.context: Stephens County is roughly two hours west and rural throughout.

counties.name: Eastland County
counties.blurb: West along I-20.
counties.context: Eastland County lies at the far western edge of a two-hour radius from the Metroplex.

counties.name: Comanche County
counties.blurb: Southwest, rural and agricultural.
counties.context: Comanche County is roughly two hours southwest of Fort Worth in predominantly agricultural country.

counties.name: Hamilton County
counties.blurb: Southwest of the Metroplex.
counties.context: Hamilton County sits at the southwestern edge of the region, rural throughout.

counties.name: Coryell County
counties.blurb: South toward the Fort Hood area.
counties.context: Coryell County lies south of the Metroplex near the Killeen area, at the outer limit of a practical service radius.

counties.name: McLennan County
counties.blurb: South along I-35, anchored by Waco.
counties.context: McLennan County centers on Waco, roughly an hour and a half south of the Dallas core along I-35, with a substantial residential base.

counties.name: Limestone County
counties.blurb: South of the Metroplex, rural.
counties.context: Limestone County is rural and sparsely populated, well south of the primary service area.

counties.name: Freestone County
counties.blurb: South along I-45.
counties.context: Freestone County sits south along the I-45 corridor toward Houston, near the practical edge of a two-hour radius.

counties.name: Bosque County
counties.blurb: Southwest along the Bosque River.
counties.context: Bosque County is rural, with Clifton and Meridian as its principal communities, south of the Fort Worth area.
